transcription.tex: \textbf{Core Pure Mathematics 1}\par Chapter 4\par Roots of Polynomials

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: This chapter relates polynomial coefficients, such as \(a,b,c\) in \(ax^2+bx+c\), to its roots: values where the polynomial is zero.
\textbf{1. Relationships for quadratics, cubics and quartics}\par Given \(kx^2+(k-3)x-2=0\), find \(k\) when the roots sum to 4.
\textbf{2. Expressions in the roots}\par Without finding the roots of \(x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0\), find the sum of their squares.
\textbf{3. Linear transformations of roots}\par If \(x^4-3x^3+15x+1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\), find an equation with roots \(2\alpha+1,2\beta+1,2\gamma+1,2\delta+1\).

transcription.tex: We want to understand how roots relate to coefficients.
What do you notice about the sum \(-2+5=3\)?
It is the negative of the coefficient of \(x\).
What do you notice about the product \((-2)(5)=-10\)?
At GCSE, factorising a monic quadratic used two numbers whose sum gives the middle coefficient and product the constant. The roots are the negatives of those factor constants.

transcription.tex: There are similar relationships for higher degrees; always assume the leading coefficient is nonzero.
Spot the pattern. What is the product of all four roots?
\(\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=e/a\).\par For a quintic the product is \(-f/a\); for a sextic it is \(g/a\). Signs alternate. These are Vieta’s formulae.

transcription.tex: 8. \(kx^2+(k-3)x-2=0\). Find \(k\) if its roots sum to 4.
The root sum is zero:\[0=\frac{16+n}{n}\Rightarrow16+n=0\Rightarrow n=-16.\]\par The resulting roots are \(\pm4\), so they are real.

transcription.tex: A cubic \(ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\), \(a\ne0\), has three roots counting multiplicity. For real coefficients, either all roots are real or one is real and two are non-real conjugates.
The sum rule matches the quadratic rule. For quadratics there is only one pair product. For cubics there is only one triple product, the product of all three roots.

transcription.tex: 8. \(2x^3-kx^2+30x-13=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).\par a. State the pair-product sum and product, and express \(k\) in terms of the roots.\par b. Given \(\alpha=2-3i\), find \(k\).
The conjugate root is \(2+3i\). Their product is 13, so \(13\gamma=13/2\Rightarrow\gamma=1/2\).\[k=2[(2-3i)+(2+3i)+1/2]=9.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 9. \(x^3-mx+n=0\) has roots \(1,-4,\alpha\).\par a. State, with a reason, whether \(\alpha\) is real.\par b. Find \(m,n,\alpha\).
It is real. A non-real root would require its distinct conjugate, in addition to the two given real roots, exceeding the degree.
The sum is zero: \(1-4+\alpha=0\Rightarrow\alpha=3\).\par Pair products: \(1(-4)+(-4)3+3(1)=-13=-m\), so \(m=13\).\par Product: \(1(-4)3=-12=-n\), so \(n=12\).

transcription.tex: 10. \(2x^3-10x^2+8x-k=0\) has root \(3-i\).\par a. Find the other roots.\par b. Find \(k\).
Another root is \(3+i\). The sum is \(10/2=5\), so \(6+\gamma=5\Rightarrow\gamma=-1\).\par The other roots are \(3+i,-1\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: From sum and pair products:\[\alpha(1+k+k^2)=14,\]\[\alpha^2k(1+k+k^2)=56.\]\par Divide the second by the first: \(\alpha k=4\). The product confirms \((\alpha k)^3=64\).
Substitute \(\alpha=4/k\) into the sum:\[\frac4k(1+k+k^2)=14\Rightarrow2k^2-5k+2=0.\]\[(2k-1)(k-2)=0.\]\par Thus \((\alpha,k)=(2,2)\) or \((8,1/2)\). Both describe roots \(2,4,8\).

transcription.tex: \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are roots of a real-coefficient cubic. Considering all real/non-real possibilities, explain why (a) their sum, (b) their pair-product sum, (c) their product are real.

transcription.tex: \(x^4+2x^3+px^2+qx-60=0\), \(p,q\in\mathbb R\), has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\), with \(\gamma=-2+4i,\delta=\gamma^*\).\par a. Show \(\alpha+\beta-2=0\), \(\alpha\beta+3=0\).\par b. Find all roots and \(p,q\).
\(\mathbb C\) denotes complex numbers. A notation such as \(\Sigma\alpha\beta\) means the sum over all distinct pairs.

The remaining roots solve \(t^2-2t-3=0\), so are \(3,-1\).\par Pair products give\[p=\alpha\beta+(\alpha+\beta)(\gamma+\delta)+\gamma\delta\]\[=-3+2(-4)+20=9.\]\par Triple products give\[-q=\alpha\beta(\gamma+\delta)+(\alpha+\beta)\gamma\delta\]\[=(-3)(-4)+2(20)=52\Rightarrow q=-52.\]\par Expanded products:\[p=3(-1)+3(-2+4i)+3(-2-4i)\]\[\quad+(-1)(-2+4i)+(-1)(-2-4i)\]\[+(-2+4i)(-2-4i)=9.\]\[-q=3(-1)(-2+4i)+3(-1)(-2-4i)\]\[\quad+(-1)(-2+4i)(-2-4i)\]\[+3(-2+4i)(-2-4i)=52.\]

transcription.tex: 8. \(x^4-16x^3+86x^2-176x+105=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\alpha+k,\alpha+2k,\alpha+3k\), with real \(k\). Solve the equation.

Root sum: \(4\alpha+6k=16\), so \(\alpha=4-3k/2\).\par The six distinct pair products are\[S_2=\alpha(\alpha+k)+\alpha(\alpha+2k)+\alpha(\alpha+3k)\]\[\quad+(\alpha+k)(\alpha+2k)+(\alpha+k)(\alpha+3k)\]\[+(\alpha+2k)(\alpha+3k)\]\[=\alpha^2+\alpha k+\alpha^2+2\alpha k+\alpha^2+3\alpha k\]\[\quad+\alpha^2+3\alpha k+2k^2\]\[+\alpha^2+4\alpha k+3k^2+\alpha^2+5\alpha k+6k^2\]\[=6\alpha^2+18\alpha k+11k^2.\]Hence\[6\alpha^2+18\alpha k+11k^2=86.\]

Substitute \(\alpha=4-3k/2\):\[6(4-3k/2)^2+18k(4-3k/2)+11k^2=86\]\[96-72k+27k^2/2+72k-27k^2+11k^2=86\]\[-5k^2/2=-10\Rightarrow k=\pm2.\]\par If \(k=2\), \(\alpha=1\), giving roots \(1,3,5,7\). If \(k=-2\), \(\alpha=7\), giving the same roots in reverse.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 9. \(3072x^4-2880x^3+840x^2-90x+3=0\) has roots \(\alpha,r\alpha,r^2\alpha,r^3\alpha\), with real \(r\). Solve the equation.

\(S_3/S_1=\alpha^2r^3=1/32\). Since \(S_1\ne0\) and \(r\) is real, \(\alpha\) is real; hence \(r>0\).\par Put \(t=r+1/r\ge2\). Then\[\frac{S_2}{\alpha^2r^3}\]\[=r^2+r+2+r^{-1}+r^{-2}\]\[=t^2+t=35/4.\]\[(2t-5)(2t+7)=0\Rightarrow t=5/2.\]\par Therefore \(r=2\) or \(1/2\). The sum gives \(\alpha=1/16\) or \(1/2\), respectively.\par All roots are \(1/16,1/8,1/4,1/2\). Their sum and products verify the coefficients.\par Sum check for \(r=\alpha=1/2\):\[\frac12\left(1+\frac12+\frac14+\frac18\right)\]\[=\frac12\cdot\frac{15}{8}=\frac{15}{16}.\]

transcription.tex: 12. \(4x^4-19x^3+px^2+qx+10=0\), with real \(p,q\), has roots \(\alpha,\beta,3+i,3-i\).\par a. Show \(4\alpha+4\beta+5=0\), \(4\alpha\beta-1=0\).\par b. Find all roots and \(p,q\).\par c. Plot the roots on an Argand diagram.
Sum: \(\alpha+\beta+6=19/4\Rightarrow\alpha+\beta=-5/4\).\par Product: \(10\alpha\beta=10/4\Rightarrow\alpha\beta=1/4\). These give the required equations.

From \(\alpha\beta=1/4\), \(\alpha=1/(4\beta)\). Substitute into \(4\alpha+4\beta+5=0\):\[1+4\beta^2+5\beta=0\]\[(4\beta+1)(\beta+1)=0.\]\par The other roots are \(-1,-1/4\). All four roots are \(-1,-1/4,3+i,3-i\).

transcription.tex: We can calculate symmetric expressions without finding individual roots. For a quadratic:\[\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta,\]\[\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}\quad(\alpha\beta\ne0).\]

\textbf{Sums of squares}\par For any number of roots, square the root sum and subtract twice the sum of distinct pair products.\par Cubic:\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=S_1^2-2S_2.\]\par Quartic:\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2=S_1^2-2S_2.\]

\textbf{Sums of cubes}\par Quadratic:\[\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta)^3-3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta).\]\par Cubic:\[\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_3.\]\par Here \(S_j\) sums distinct products of \(j\) roots. These results may be used without proof.
The same symmetric-sum pattern extends to higher degrees. A quartic sum-of-cubes formula is not required in this chapter.

transcription.tex: Without finding the roots \(\alpha,\beta\) of \(x^2-3x-10=0\), find an equation with roots \(\alpha-1,\beta-1\).\par \textbf{Method 1: coefficients}
Original sum \(3\), product \(-10\).\par New sum: \((\alpha-1)+(\beta-1)=3-2=1\).\par New product:\[(\alpha-1)(\beta-1)=\alpha\beta-\alpha-\beta+1\]\[=-10-3+1=-12.\]\par Hence \(w^2-w-12=0\).
\textbf{Method 2: substitution}\par Use a new variable for the transformed root.
This is the familiar function transformation: translating roots left by 1 means using \(f(w+1)\). Substitution is generally the simpler method.

transcription.tex: \textbf{What do sums and products tell us?}\par They connect the geometry of roots with polynomial coefficients. The mean of \(n\) roots is \(S_1/n\); on an Argand diagram this is the centroid of their points, counting multiplicity.\par For \(z^k=a+ib\), integer \(k\ge2\), the sum of the roots is zero because the coefficient of \(z^{k-1}\) is zero.

\textbf{Why is this useful?}\par If one root is missing, subtract the known roots from \(-b/a\). If a coefficient is unknown, use information about the roots to determine it. These relationships strengthen our ability to reason about polynomials.

\textbf{Why sums of squares or reciprocals?}\par They let us evaluate expressions without solving for individual roots, and form equations for transformed roots. This algebraic structure remains useful even when no immediate physical application is given.
